hood_landmark.District 1: Ben Thanh Market and the French-colonial Notre-Dame Cathedral quarter
hood_landmark.District 3: The War Remnants Museum and its outdoor military exhibits
hood_landmark.Cholon (District 5): Thien Hau Temple in the heart of historic Chinatown
hood_landmark.Thao Dien (District 2): Riverside expat enclave of cafes, boutiques and international eateries
hood_landmark.Phu My Hung (District 7): Starlight (Anh Sao) Bridge and the Crescent lakeside promenade

avoid.reason: Motorbike bag-/phone-snatching (esp. District 1/Pham Ngu Lao) and taxi-meter scams — use Grab; pickpocketing

hood_desc: District 1 is the central business and tourist heart, home to Ben Thanh Market, the Dong Khoi luxury strip, rooftop bars and the Pham Ngu Lao backpacker zone. It suits first-time visitors and business travelers who want to be walkable to the main sights.

District 3 sits right beside District 1 but feels calmer, with leafy tree-lined streets, French-era villas, Turtle Lake and a strong local cafe and dining scene. It appeals to travelers who want a central yet more authentic, residential base.

Cholon in District 5 is the historic Chinatown, a bustling maze of wholesale markets like Binh Tay, ornate pagodas and outstanding cheap street food. It suits culture seekers and foodies who do not mind chaos and crowds over polish.

Thao Dien in Thu Duc City, the former District 2, is the leafy riverside expat enclave packed with international restaurants, boutiques, wine bars and cafes. It draws expats, families and digital nomads wanting green quiet and Western comforts a short ride from downtown.

Phu My Hung in District 7 is a modern master-planned district with wide clean boulevards, malls, international schools and a large Korean and Taiwanese community. It suits families and long-stay visitors who prefer orderly, suburban calm away from the dense center.

water.note: Avoid tap water; use bottled or boiled water, even for brushing teeth.

transit.pay: Buy a reusable Stored Fare Card at station machines/counters, or tap a contactless Visa/Mastercard/NAPAS bank card directly at the gates; MoMo, ZaloPay and the HCMC Metro app also work. Single rides cost 7,000-20,000 VND (about $0.30-0.80); a 1-day pass is 40,000 VND (~$1.60).
transit.hours: Line 1 runs daily about 5am-10pm with trains every 8-12 minutes; there is no overnight service.

food.name: Com tam
food.desc: Saigon's own plate of broken rice with a charcoal-grilled pork chop, shredded pork skin, steamed egg meatloaf and sweet fish sauce.

places.name: Com Tam Ba Ghien
places.note: Queues down the street for an outsized grilled chop; a Saigon rite of passage.

places.name: Com Tam Nguyen Van Cu
places.note: Michelin-noted for a soulful version with pork skin and steamed egg casserole.

food.name: Banh mi
food.desc: Airy Saigon baguette split and loaded with pate, cold cuts, pickled carrot and daikon, cucumber, coriander and chilli.

places.name: Banh Mi Huynh Hoa
places.note: Open since 1989; house pate and mayo, and a queue that spills into the road.

places.name: Banh Mi Bay Ho
places.note: Old-school stall famous for its house-made cha lua and grilled pork.

food.name: Hu tieu Nam Vang
food.desc: Clear pork-and-shrimp noodle soup brought by the Chinese-Cambodian diaspora, served dry or in broth with quail eggs and crisp shallots.

places.name: Hu Tieu Nam Vang Hong Phat
places.note: Reputedly the city's first Nam Vang shop, open since the 1970s.

places.name: Hu Tieu Nam Vang Ty Lum
places.note: Chinatown veteran; order it kho (dry) with the broth alongside.

food.name: Banh xeo
food.desc: A huge turmeric-yellow rice crepe crackling with pork, whole prawns and bean sprouts, torn up and wrapped in lettuce and herbs.

places.name: Banh Xeo 46A
places.note: Michelin Bib Gourmand; an ultra-thin crepe with an egg cracked in mid-cook.

places.name: Banh Xeo An La Ghien
places.note: Air-conditioned and easy for first-timers, with mushroom and vegetarian versions.

food.name: Oc
food.desc: The Saigon evening ritual: sea snails, clams, scallops and razor shells grilled or stir-fried with tamarind, coconut, garlic and chilli.

places.name: Vinh Khanh Street
places.note: An entire street of snail restaurants, plastic stools and beer, buzzing from 6pm.

places.name: Oc Dao
places.note: Long-running alley favourite among locals for grilled scallops and tamarind snails.

food.name: Pho Saigon-style
food.desc: Sweeter and more herbaceous than the northern original, served with a mountain of basil and bean sprouts plus hoisin and chilli sauce.

places.name: Pho Hoa Pasteur
places.note: Open since 1968 and still the city's benchmark bowl; free youtiao on the table.

places.name: Pho Le
places.note: Cholon institution with a deeply beefy broth and rare-beef bowls that sell out early.

food.name: Ca phe sua da
food.desc: Robusta coffee dripped through a phin filter onto condensed milk and ice: dark, syrupy and strong enough to reset the afternoon.

places.name: Cheo Leo Cafe
places.note: Brewing in cloth socks since 1938; the oldest working cafe in the city.

places.name: The Cafe Apartment
places.note: A whole 1960s apartment block of cafes; ride the lift and pick a balcony.

food.name: Bia hoi and Saigon craft beer
food.desc: Cheap fresh-brewed draught poured at street level, alongside a serious craft scene using passionfruit, jasmine and Vietnamese cacao.

places.name: Pasteur Street Brewing Original Taproom
places.note: Vietnam's pioneering craft brewery; the Jasmine IPA is the one to order.

places.name: Bui Vien Walking Street
places.note: Street-side plastic stools and cheap draught, loud and chaotic after dark.

landmarks: Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica of Saigon
A striking twin-spired French colonial-era brick cathedral in the city center that's one of the most photographed buildings in Vietnam.
Saigon Central Post Office
A grand 19th-century colonial post office with an ornate vaulted interior designed in a style associated with Gustave Eiffel's era.
Independence Palace
The former presidential palace of South Vietnam, famous as the site where a tank crashed through its gates ending the Vietnam War in 1975.
Bến Thành Market
The city's iconic clock-tower market entrance is a classic symbol of Saigon, bustling with color, food stalls, and street life.
Bitexco Financial Tower
A sleek 68-story skyscraper with a distinctive cantilevered helipad disc, offering a striking silhouette against the skyline.
War Remnants Museum
A powerful museum displaying military hardware and war photography that offers a moving, historically significant photo subject.
Jade Emperor Pagoda
A century-old Taoist temple filled with smoky incense, intricate carvings, and statues, offering an atmospheric, colorful photo opportunity.
Củ Chi Tunnels
A vast underground tunnel network used during the Vietnam War, offering a unique and historically vivid photo experience just outside the city.
Ho Chi Minh City Opera House
An elegant French colonial theatre with an ornately decorated facade, illuminated beautifully at night.
Thien Hau Temple of Cholon
A vibrant 19th-century Chinese temple in Cholon known for its spiraling incense coils hanging from the ceiling, a favorite photo subject.

train.note: No international trains from the south - Vietnam's only cross-border rail runs from Hanoi to China, and that service has been intermittent. Sai Gon station in District 3 is the southern terminus of the Reunification Express, with trains to Nha Trang in about 7 hours, Da Nang in 16 and Hanoi in 32. Soft sleeper is the class to book. Buy on dsvn.vn or through Baolau; the line runs close to the coast for much of the way and is a genuinely scenic journey.

intl.to: Phnom Penh (Cambodia) - via the Moc Bai border, ~6-7 hr

bus.note: The Phnom Penh coaches are straightforward and popular: about six to seven hours including the Moc Bai/Bavet border, where you get off with your luggage for stamps. Most nationalities can get a Cambodian visa on arrival, but check first. Domestic sleeper buses to Da Lat, Mui Ne and the Mekong Delta leave from Mien Dong and Mien Tay terminals or from the operators' own offices in District 1; book through Vexere (https://vexere.com/) or Baolau.

intl.to: Vung Tau (Vietnam) - hydrofoil down the Saigon River, ~2 hr
Mekong Delta towns & Phnom Penh (Cambodia) - multi-day river cruise
intl.op: river cruise operators — booked through travel agents

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry, though slow-boat Mekong river cruises do run through to Phnom Penh as a packaged trip rather than a timetabled service. The Vung Tau hydrofoil from Bach Dang pier is the useful local route, reaching the beach town in about two hours and avoiding the traffic on the road. Sailings are cancelled in rough conditions.

half.name: Cu Chi Tunnels
half.country: Cu Chi, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
half.blurb: Vast underground network from the war years, now open for crawling through and learning history.

half.name: Mekong Delta
half.blurb: Lush river country of floating markets, coconut groves, and sampan cruises through palm-lined canals.

half.name: Vung Tau
half.blurb: Breezy coastal town with beaches, seafood, and a hilltop Jesus statue overlooking the sea.

half.name: Cao Dai Temple and Ba Den Mountain
half.blurb: Kaleidoscopic Cao Dai temple pairs with a cable car up the province's highest peak.

half.name: Can Gio Mangrove Forest
half.country: Can Gio, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
half.blurb: Protected biosphere of tidal mangroves, monkeys, and boat rides through a wild coastal wetland.

full.name: Nam Cat Tien National Park
full.blurb: Sprawling rainforest reserve rich with birds, gibbons, ancient trees, and jungle walking trails.
